title: The Simple Slide I Use to Structure My Lessons
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart lays out the simple beginning-middles-end slide template he uses daily to structure lessons, then spends most of the article explaining the intentional purpose behind each part rather than presenting the template as a plug-and-play tool. The warm-up nearly always takes the same form, provisional writing, because that consistency does specific social, intellectual, and emotional work beyond just occupying students at the bell. The middle of class is always built from a small, fixed set of moves (key beliefs, knowledge-building, argument, reading, writing, speaking/listening) drawn from his book These 6 Things, and he argues that mastery of a few moves used repeatedly beats novelty. He closes with an explicit caveat: the slide format only works if a teacher understands the reasoning behind each part, since the structure itself contains no magic and cannot substitute for that understanding.
points: Stuart's central caveat, that "the power isn't in the tool, it's in the user," pushes back against readers who might copy his slide template without understanding the reasoning behind each section.

His near-constant warm-up choice, provisional writing, is deliberately chosen for compounding benefits (focus, visible student thinking, room-settling, writing volume) rather than variety for its own sake.
He deliberately limits his instructional repertoire to six recurring moves from These 6 Things, arguing that depth of practice with a few tools beats breadth across many.
quotes: Now like any tool, the power isn't in the tool, it's in the user. If you go and copy this format and don't understand what you're doing or why you're doing it, it won't do you much good.
Emotionally, it lets students know what to expect when class starts, which creates the safety that comes through consistency.
95% of the time, I have them do the same exact thing: provisional writing. It's hard. It requires focus. It unlocks thinking.
These are always some variation of the basic moves I write about in These 6 Things: key beliefs, knowledge-building, argument, reading, writing, speaking and listening.

Those are the only things I am good at using to develop student mastery. But, because there are so few things and because I've been studying and practicing them for so long, I've become excellent at weaving them together to make functional, enjoyable lessons.
What I hope you notice in this brief article is that my simple slides hide a lot of intentionality and strategy. The slide isn't magic.

You can't lean on the slides to help you. You've got to understand what you and the students are doing, why you're doing these things, and the simple moves that help these things produce as much learning as possible in a given day.
